claims.text: The distribution and stability of nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates govern high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in tungsten-based fusion plasma-facing components.
The as-processed tungsten alloy has a characteristic nanoscale precipitate distribution along its grain boundaries.
Thermal annealing can coarsen or partially dissolve the grain-boundary precipitates without changing bulk chemistry.
Temperatures of approximately 1200–1500°C represent fusion-relevant high-temperature mechanical-test conditions for the proposed tungsten materials.
At elevated temperatures, nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates pin dislocations.
Restricting dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding enhances toughness.
Restricting dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding reduces high-temperature plastic strain rates.
Changes in precipitate size, distribution, or volume fraction alter the ease of high-temperature plastic deformation.
Annealed specimens with disrupted precipitate networks will exhibit more high-temperature plastic strain than the unperturbed baseline.
Annealed specimens with disrupted precipitate networks will exhibit lower toughness than the unperturbed baseline.
Fewer or larger precipitates are less effective obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding.
The original baseline precipitate distribution is optimally distributed.
The proposed mechanism applies below 1500°C when radiation damage is negligible, precipitate coarsening or dissolution is operative, and no additional phase changes occur.
Neutron irradiation or plasma interactions may alter precipitate stability.
Impurity segregation may contribute significantly to high-temperature mechanical behavior.
